name: Guarayu
confidence_why: Danielsen's 2019 orthography article, its 2020 reprint and the Spanish and English introductions to the revised Hoeller dictionary by Danielsen, Sell and Terhart all give the same three-way dialect split (Urubichá penultimate, Ascensión mostly final, Yaguarú sometimes antepenultimate), but they are a single fieldworker's hedged descriptive statements with no second independent description of Guarayu stress to confirm them.

catalog_quote: There are three varieties that differ in stress placement and vocabulary, as well as pronunciation of a number of words; the varieties spoken in Urubichá and Salvatierra have penultimate word stress, the dialect that is spoken in the department’s capital Ascensión de Guarayos, as well as in San Pablo and Yotaú, has predominant final stress, and speakers of the Yaguarú and Cururú dialect place stress sometimes on the antepenultimate syllable. ... Since stress placement is one of the decisive factors that distinguishes the three main dialects of the language (Urubichá – Ascensión – Yaguarú), it has been decided (Aeguazu et al. 2003) not to encode word accent in the orthographic system ... This decision does not pose a problem for speakers of the Urubichá dialect that usually has penultimate stress just like Spanish. However, some people from Ascensión feel discriminated by this decision, …

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every segment of the deciding quotation and the exq_/the secondary-stress rule snippets are verbatim in the Dictionaria text we hold at the stated sections (intro para 1; Orthography paragraphs on stress and nasality). Deciding source: a dictionary introduction (Dictionaria, Danielsen, Sell & Terhart, 2019/2022) — first-hand and current, by the language's main fieldworker, but descriptive prose with hedges ('usually', 'predominant', 'sometimes'), not a phonological analysis. Corroboration: the held Dietrich & Danielsen 2024 edition (pp.22, 34, 37) and the now-downloaded Danielsen 2019 (Página y Signos p.124) and Gwarayu Ñe'ësa 2-3 restate the same three-way dialect split (Urubichá penultimate, Ascensión mostly final, Yaguarú partly antepenultimate) and the nasal-attracts-stress generalisation, so the 'variable' (dialect-split, right-edge) coding is well supported and nothing found contradicts it.

sources.quote: Same text as the deciding source in Spanish: Urubichá/Salvatierra penultimate, Ascensión/San Pablo/Yotaú 'acento final mayormente', Yaguarú 'a menudo' antepenultimate; nasal syllable generally carries stress; Urubichá 'la penúltima sílaba lleva regularmente el acento, a pesar de la nasalidad'.

sources.citation: Danielsen, Swintha. 2019. Las ortografías del guarayu: historia y actualidad. Página y Signos (Cochabamba) 15: 89-131 [Zenodo 8373354].
sources.quote: 'Aquí tenemos tres dialectos diferentes que justamente se distinguen por la colocación del acento. En el dialecto de Ascensión el acento cae más a menudo en la última sílaba, en Urubichá en la penúltima (como en castellano), y en Yaguarú el acento cae a veces en la antepenúltima sílaba. Así junto con la aprobación del alfabeto, los Guarayo han votado por no indicar el acento en ninguno de los dialectos.' Also p.124-125: 'la nasal siempre atrae el acento ... (característica tupí-guaraní)'.
No stress statements (texts, lexicon, community material).

sources.note: Second-hand database coding: SAPhon v2.1.0 lists the Guarayu (gyr) inventory (17 consonants, 6 oral + 6 nasal vowels) with the field 'Suprasegmental: None'; the underlying data file (SAPhon-ling/saphon GitHub, langs/Guarayu.yaml, doctype synthesis) codes explicitly 'tone: False', 'nasal_harmony: False', 'laryngeal_harmony: False', sourced to Armoye Urarepia 2009 (tesina, Ms.) and Ureyu 2003 (alphabet guide). It is a thin coding (no stress or nasal-spreading information) but an explicit no-tone record.

sources.note: The only peer-reviewed phonology article on Guarayu (47 pp, includes a speech-perception experiment), by a metrical-stress specialist with Guarayu fieldwork; its phonological background section almost certainly states the stress rule for the variety studied with more precision than the dictionary introduction our classification rests on (regularity of penultimate stress, any weight/nasality or morphological conditioning). Not in Glottolog's list; not yet obtained.
